overview.para1: East Asian cuisine covers a diverse range of food traditions from China, Korea, Japan and surrounding regions. Rice, noodles, vegetables, seafood, fermented foods and broths are common, with dishes often built around fresh ingredients and carefully balanced flavours.
overview.para2: Many dishes are naturally based around rice, vegetables and fresh proteins, which can make some meals easier to adapt. However, sauces, marinades, dumplings and processed ingredients can introduce several common allergens, so the preparation of a dish is often just as important as its main ingredients.

triggers.examples: Soy sauce, tofu, miso, tempeh, edamame
Soy sauce, wheat noodles, dumpling wrappers, marinades
Sesame oil, sesame seeds, sesame-based sauces
Fish sauce, dried fish, fish-based broths
Prawns, shrimp paste, dried shrimp
Oysters, squid, mussels in soups and stir-fries
Egg noodles, fried rice, omelettes, dumplings

safeDefaults.caveat: ask for no sauce or sesame oil

closingTip: Ask what's in the sauce, marinade and broth — that's where most hidden triggers appear.

overview.para1: South Asian cuisine spans a wide range of traditions including those of Bangladesh, India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka and neighbouring regions. Rice, wheat, lentils, vegetables, spices, yoghurt, eggs, fish and meat all feature prominently.
overview.para2: The large number of naturally plant-based dishes can make South Asian food surprisingly adaptable. The main challenge is that sauces, breads, spice blends and fried foods can contain several triggers at once, while dairy and wheat are particularly common in certain dishes.

triggers.examples: Yoghurt, ghee, cream, paneer, milk-based desserts
Roti, naan, chapati, paratha, samosas
Peanuts, peanut-based sauces and garnishes
Cashews, almonds in sauces and desserts
Sesame seeds in chutneys and some breads
Lentils, chickpeas, peas, beans
Fresh and dried chilli in curries and chutneys

closingTip: Ask whether a curry contains cream, yoghurt, ghee or nuts, and check breads separately — a simple-looking dish can hide several triggers in its sauce.

overview.para1: South East Asian cuisine brings together the food traditions of countries including Thailand, Vietnam, Malaysia, Indonesia and the Philippines. Rice, noodles, fresh herbs, vegetables, seafood, tropical fruit and intensely flavoured sauces are central to many dishes.
overview.para2: Fresh ingredients and rice-based dishes can provide relatively simple options, but sauces and pastes are important to watch. Soy, fish, shellfish, peanuts, wheat and chilli can appear together in a single meal, particularly in restaurant cooking.

triggers.examples: Soy sauce, tofu, fermented soy, marinades
Fish sauce, dried fish, fish paste
Prawns, shrimp paste, dried shrimp
Peanut sauce, satay, crushed peanuts
Wheat noodles, soy sauce, spring-roll wrappers
Sesame seeds and sesame oil as toppings
Fresh chilli, dried chilli, chilli paste

closingTip: The dipping sauce can matter more than the dish itself — always ask what's in sauces, pastes and marinades.

overview.para1: Mediterranean cuisine covers the diverse food traditions surrounding the Mediterranean Sea, including Southern Europe, the Middle East and North Africa. Fresh vegetables, fruit, grains, legumes, herbs, olive oil, fish and meat feature heavily.
overview.para2: Many Mediterranean meals are built from simple ingredients served separately, which can make them easier to adapt. However, wheat, dairy, fish, shellfish, sesame, mustard and sulphites can occur in breads, cheeses, sauces, preserved foods and restaurant dishes.

triggers.examples: Bread, pasta, couscous, pastries, pizza
Cheese, yoghurt, cream, dairy-based sauces
Fresh and preserved fish dishes
Prawns and shrimp in seafood dishes
Tahini, sesame seeds, sesame-based sauces
Dressings, sauces, marinades
Wine, dried fruit, preserved foods

closingTip: Mediterranean menus often let you control ingredients individually — ordering grilled foods with sides on the side makes it easier to avoid specific triggers.

overview.para1: South American cuisine reflects the food traditions of a vast continent, combining Indigenous ingredients with European, African and Asian influences. Corn, rice, potatoes, beans, fresh vegetables, fruit, meat and seafood are important across many regions.
overview.para2: Many traditional meals are centred around naturally simple ingredients such as rice, corn, potatoes and grilled meats. Wheat, dairy, peanuts, seafood and onion can become more important in breads, pastries, sauces and regional specialities.

triggers.examples: Bread, pastries, pasta, empanada dough
Cheese, milk, cream, dairy desserts
Peanuts in sauces and sweets in some regions
Fresh fish and ceviche
Prawns and shrimp in coastal dishes
Raw and cooked onion in sauces, stews, ceviche
Fresh and dried chilli in sauces

closingTip: Look for meals built around one or two simple ingredients rather than heavily sauced dishes — recipes vary a lot by country, so always check preparation.

overview.para1: West African cuisine includes the diverse food traditions of countries such as Ghana, Nigeria, Senegal and Côte d'Ivoire. Rice, cassava, plantain, yams, beans, vegetables, fish and meat form the foundation of many dishes, with aromatic sauces and stews providing much of the flavour.
overview.para2: Many traditional dishes use naturally simple staples, particularly rice, root vegetables and plantain. Peanuts, fish, shellfish, tomato, onion, garlic and chilli are nevertheless common in sauces and stews, making the accompanying sauce especially important to check.

triggers.examples: Peanut stews, sauces, groundnut dishes
Fresh, dried and smoked fish
Prawns and shrimp in coastal soups
Tomato-based sauces, stews, rice dishes
A common base for stews and sauces
Used with onion in marinades and sauces
Fresh and dried chilli for heat and flavour
Less central, but appears in drinks and desserts

closingTip: The staple and the sauce are usually separate — asking for the plain staple without the stew makes choosing much easier if you have several triggers.

overview.para1: North African cuisine includes the rich food traditions of Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya and Egypt. Grains, vegetables, legumes, fruit, meat, fish and aromatic herbs and spices are used extensively, with dishes often built around slow-cooked stews, breads and couscous.
overview.para2: Simple grilled meats, vegetables and rice-based dishes can be relatively easy to adapt, but wheat, dairy, sesame, nuts, fish and sulphites can occur in breads, sauces, preserved foods and desserts.

triggers.examples: Couscous, breads, pastries, flatbreads
Yoghurt, cheese, butter, desserts
Almonds in tagines, couscous, pastries
Sesame seeds in breads and sweets
Common in coastal North African cooking
Dried fruit and preserved ingredients
Chilli and chilli pastes

safeDefaults.caveat: check the marinade and spice blend
check the base for onion, garlic, chilli

closingTip: Couscous is wheat-based, not a rice substitute — if gluten or wheat is a concern, ask what grain has actually been used.

overview.para1: East African cuisine brings together food traditions from countries including Ethiopia, Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda and surrounding regions. Grains, maize, rice, legumes, vegetables, meat, fish and aromatic spices feature prominently, with considerable variation between countries.
overview.para2: Many meals are built around naturally simple staples such as rice, maize, potatoes and vegetables. However, wheat, milk, legumes, sesame, fish, onion, garlic and chilli can appear frequently depending on the regional dish.

triggers.examples: Chapati, breads, pastries, snacks
Milk, yoghurt, butter, dairy drinks
Lentils, beans, peas in many dishes
Seeds and sesame-based ingredients in some breads
Fresh, dried and smoked fish, especially coastal
A base for stews, sauces, vegetable dishes
Used in meat, vegetable and stew preparations

closingTip: Food varies a lot by country and community here — start with a plain staple and add individually checked foods rather than choosing a heavily mixed dish.

overview.para1: Southern African cuisine reflects Indigenous traditions alongside Dutch, Malay, Indian and other influences. Maize, meat, vegetables, beans, potatoes, rice and fruit are common, with grilling, stewing and slow cooking used extensively.
overview.para2: Simple grilled meat, maize-based foods, vegetables and fresh fruit can provide straightforward choices. More complex dishes may contain dairy, wheat, mustard, tomato, onion, garlic, chilli or sulphites depending on the recipe and regional influence.

triggers.examples: Milk, cheese, butter, cream, desserts
Bread, pastries, baked and processed foods
Marinades, sauces, dressings
Sauces, relishes, stews, marinades
Common in stews, gravies, relishes
Used in marinades, sauces, meat dishes
Some preserved foods, dried fruit, wine

closingTip: Grilled food looks simple, but marinades, basting sauces and condiments often carry several triggers — ask for them separately where you can.

overview.para1: Central African cuisine encompasses a wide range of traditions across countries including Cameroon, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the Republic of the Congo and surrounding regions. Cassava, plantain, maize, rice, vegetables, legumes, fish and meat are important staples.
overview.para2: Many traditional meals are based on simple starchy staples served alongside vegetable, meat or fish dishes. Peanuts, fish, shellfish, tomato, onion, garlic and chilli are common in sauces and stews, so the accompanying dish often determines which triggers need attention.

triggers.examples: Peanut sauces, stews, groundnut dishes
Fresh, dried and smoked fish
Prawns and shrimp in coastal or river dishes
Used in sauces, stews, vegetable dishes
A common flavour base
Used in marinades, sauces, stews
Fresh and dried chilli in sauces
Beans and other pulses in traditional meals

closingTip: Dishes are often a simple staple plus a richly flavoured sauce — ask for the staple separately and check the sauce if you need to minimise triggers.

overview.para1: Western fast food covers the everyday staples of burger bars, fish and chip shops, diners and pancake houses. Fried and battered foods, bread, dairy and rich sauces are central, with speed and convenience often meaning less visibility into exactly how something is prepared.
overview.para2: A few naturally simple options exist, such as plain grilled meat or a jacket potato, but shared fryers and standard recipes mean many dishes carry several common allergens at once, often in the batter, bun or sauce rather than the headline ingredient.

triggers.examples: Burger buns, batter, breadcrumbs, pancakes
Cheese, milkshakes, butter, cream, mayonnaise
Batter, pancakes, mayonnaise, some sauces
Fried fish, fish in shared fryer oil
Prawns in shared fryers or seafood sides
Burger sauces, mayonnaise, condiments
Sesame-topped buns
Some soft drinks, processed sauces, syrups

closingTip: Ask what the batter, bun and shared fryer oil contain — in fast food, the frying process often carries more triggers than the ingredient list suggests.
